blocks.text:
Michelle Roberts
Chief Financial Officer
Dyer and Sons
Dear Ms. Roberts,

Thank you for asking us to review the property before Dyer and Sons commits to the purchase. This letter sets out the terms on which we will carry out a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}, and it records in writing what we discussed by telephone last week. I have kept it plain, because you should know exactly what you are engaging us to do before any work begins. Please read it through, and if any part of it differs from what you expected, call me and we will settle it before you sign.
The Assessment We Will Carry Out

A Phase I assessment is a review of a property's environmental history and its present condition. We conduct it to the current ASTM standard, E1527-13, which is the practice a lender or a buyer will expect us to have followed. The purpose is to identify recognized environmental conditions, the term of art for evidence that a release of a hazardous substance has occurred, is occurring, or is likely to have occurred on the property. Where we find such evidence we will say so, and where we do not, we will say that as well.

The work falls into a records review, a site visit, and a set of interviews, and the report draws the three together. We examine historical aerial photographs, fire-insurance maps, chain-of-title material, and any prior environmental reports on the property. We commission a regulatory database search covering the parcel and the sites around it, and we read what the federal and state records show about the property and its neighbors. One of our scientists then walks the site and photographs what is there, and we speak with people who know its history. None of this involves sampling soil or groundwater. A Phase I is a paper-and-observation study, and if it turns up a condition that warrants testing, that testing is a separate piece of work we would scope with you at the time.
Who Will Do the Work

I will oversee the engagement and sign the report that reaches you, and I read every report before it leaves this office. James Henderson, one of our environmental scientists, will lead the records review and the regulatory research and will write the assessment; the desk work behind a Phase I is his particular strength. Mary Foster, our field technician, will conduct the site reconnaissance and keep the photographic record. John Sanchez, our senior scientist, will review the findings before I do, and he will tell me plainly if the record does not support a conclusion. Between us you have the whole of the firm's technical bench on this file.
Fee and Schedule

We will carry out the assessment for a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2016-001.fee}}, which covers the records review, the regulatory database search, the site visit, the interviews, and the written report. The fee does not move with the findings, so you know the cost of the work at the outset. We are ready to begin on {{fact:f:E-2016-001.start}}, and we expect to have the report to you approximately four months after we start, allowing for the turnaround of the regulatory database search and the records we request from third parties. If anything in the file threatens that timing, you will hear it from me early, not at the end.
Fees and Payment

We invoice the fixed fee in two parts: half on your signing of this letter, and the balance on delivery of the report. Invoices are payable within thirty days of the date they carry. Any direct costs we arrange on your behalf, such as the regulatory database subscription or the retrieval of archived records, are included in the fixed fee and are not billed separately, so there is nothing unexpected on a later statement.
Term and Termination

The engagement begins when you sign this letter and ends when we deliver the report and you have paid for it. Either of us may end it earlier on written notice. If you end it before we finish, we will bill you for the work completed to that point and hand over what we have produced. If we end it, which we would do only for a reason we could explain to you, we will not bill for work left undone.
Confidentiality

We treat what we learn about the property and about Dyer and Sons as yours, and we do not discuss your business with anyone outside the engagement without your consent. The report is prepared for your use and for the lender or counsel you name to us. We keep our working file for the period our professional standards require, and we release it to no one else without your instruction or a lawful demand we cannot refuse.
Limitation of Liability

A Phase I assessment reduces uncertainty; it does not remove it. It reflects the records that exist and are reasonably ascertainable, the condition of the property on the day we see it, and the recollections of the people we interview, and it cannot account for what those sources do not disclose. For that reason our liability arising out of this engagement is limited to the amount of the fee, except where the law does not permit such a limit. This is the ordinary term for work of this kind, and I am glad to talk it through if it gives you pause.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which the property lies, and any dispute under it will be resolved in the courts of that state. We would of course try to settle any disagreement between us directly before it reached that point.

If these terms match your understanding, please sign both copies of this letter and return one to me, and we will begin the assessment on the date named above. I am glad to be working with you on this, and please feel free to call me directly at any point while the work is underway.

To: James Henderson, John Sanchez
From: Mary Foster
Re: Kickoff, Phase I Site Assessment for Dyer and Sons

We have the Phase I for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}. Work begins on {{fact:f:E-2016-001.start}}. The client needs a defensible assessment to ASTM E1527-13 before it closes on the property, and our job is to give them one on the schedule set in the engagement letter.

This is a property review, not a sampling job. We identify recognized environmental conditions if they exist, and we document their absence if they do not. We do not test soil or groundwater on a Phase I. If the review turns up something that warrants testing, that is a separate scope we raise with the client, and we do not start it on our own.

The client contact is Michelle Roberts, their Chief Financial Officer. Anything that needs a client decision goes to her through the engagement lead, not straight from the field. Keep client questions off your own email and route them up.
How the Work Breaks Down
Five streams, roughly in this order.

items: Records review. Historical aerials, fire-insurance maps, chain of title, city directories, and any prior environmental reports on the property. James Henderson owns this and runs it back through the standard look-back period.
Regulatory database search. Federal and state listings for the property and the sites around it. I order it first, because the vendor turnaround is the long pole on this schedule.
Site reconnaissance. A full walk of the property with a photo log keyed to a site sketch. I run this and set the date once we have access.
Interviews. The current owner, the site manager, and anyone local who knows the history. Split between James and me, with the notes written up the same day.
Report and review. James drafts to E1527-13, John Sanchez reviews the findings, and the report goes up for signature before it leaves the office.

blocks.text: The deliverable is one report to the client, with our finding stated plainly: either we found no recognized environmental conditions, or we found one and we say what it is. There is no interim report. Everything lands in the final document, so the record behind it has to be complete.
First Moves
I will order the regulatory database search on day one so the clock starts. James begins pulling the historical record the same week. Neither task waits on the other.

I need site access confirmed before I can schedule the reconnaissance. Once the client gives us a date and a point of contact on the ground, I will circulate a field plan with access notes and what to bring. Plan for field conditions; parts of these estuary parcels sit low and hold water.

I am setting up the project file today. Photographs get logged with station, date, and direction on the day they are taken, and interview notes go in under the interviewee and the date. If it is not written down and dated, we cannot use it in the report.

The schedule is tight but ordinary for this scope. The database turnaround and the client's records are the two things that can move the schedule, and I am pushing on both early so they do not stack up at the end. Questions on scope come to me before we start, not after.
Attendees

items: Michelle Roberts, Chief Financial Officer, Dyer and Sons

blocks.text: The short version, which we gave Michelle at the top of the meeting, is that the assessment is proceeding without surprises, and nothing found so far would change the scope or the schedule we set for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}. What follows is the detail behind that. We met to walk the client through where the records and the field work stand and to line up the interviews that close out the look-back.

On timing, we told Michelle that the work is tracking to the schedule in the engagement letter and remains within the agreed fee. Neither the records review nor the reconnaissance has surfaced anything that would add cost, and we would flag it at once if that changed.
Records and Regulatory Review

James walked us through the records review. The historical aerials and the title chain are in hand, and they show the sequence of uses we would expect for a parcel of this age. We noted one earlier use that we want to run down further before we characterize it, which is ordinary caution rather than a concern.

The regulatory database search has come back, and the property itself carries no listing. Two neighboring sites do appear, both up-gradient of the parcel, and we spent some time on what that could mean. Our present reading is that neither is likely to have affected the subject property, but we agreed to keep the question open until James has read the file on the nearer of the two.

We also settled the interview plan. James and Mary will speak with the current owner and the site manager, and we asked Michelle to help us reach a former manager who worked the property for many years. The value of that conversation is the memory it carries, the uses and small incidents that rarely reach a public record.
Site Reconnaissance

Mary reported on the site visit. The walk is complete and the photographic log is filed; nothing on the surface suggested a release, no stained soil, no distressed vegetation, no drums or fill of concern. The log is keyed to a site sketch, so each photograph can be placed on the property later without relying on memory.

She did flag a former equipment area at the rear of the site. There is nothing on the surface there that concerns us, but the ground is worth a second, careful look, and we will photograph it once more when we return for the interviews so that the record is complete.
Client Items

Michelle confirmed that Dyer and Sons will provide the older ownership records and the name of a long-standing site manager we can interview. We were grateful for that. Those two items are usually the hardest for us to obtain on our own, and having them from the client shortens the tail of the work.
Action Items

rows: Read the regulatory file on the nearer up-gradient site
Complete the follow-up walk of the rear equipment area
Provide archived ownership records and site-manager contact
Consolidate findings and confirm no change to scope

blocks.text: We agreed to meet again once the interviews are done, when James expects to have a first draft of the assessment in shape for review. Minutes recorded by John Sanchez.

This report covers progress on the Phase I Environmental Site Assessment we are conducting for {{fact:f:E-2016-001.client}}, prepared for the Dyer and Sons management team. It reflects the work through the first half of the engagement.
Where the Work Stands

The assessment is on schedule and within budget. We are roughly at the midpoint of the engagement. The records and regulatory review is substantially complete, and the site reconnaissance is done. No condition has come to light that would enlarge the scope of the work or change what we expect to deliver.

The work remains within the fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2016-001.fee}}. We do not anticipate additional cost. Nothing found so far points toward the separate sampling program that a Phase I sometimes recommends, and if that changes we will tell you before we do any further work.
Completed This Period

James Henderson has completed the historical records review. That included the aerial photographs, the chain of title, the fire-insurance maps, city directories, and the prior environmental reports we could obtain for the property. Together these establish how the parcel has been used back through the standard look-back period.

The regulatory database search has been received and read. It covered the standard federal and state lists at the search distances the ASTM practice prescribes: the National Priorities List, the federal and state records of contaminated and formerly contaminated sites, registered and leaking underground storage tanks, and reported spills. We read each listing within those distances and plotted the mapped sites against the property and the local groundwater gradient.

The property itself carries no environmental listing on the federal or state records. Two neighboring sites do appear, both up-gradient of the parcel; James Henderson is reviewing the file on the nearer of the two so that we can state plainly whether either bears on the property.

Our field technician, Mary Foster, completed the site reconnaissance and the photographic log. The surface walk found no evidence of a release: no stained soils, no stressed vegetation, no improper storage of drums or chemicals. A former equipment area at the rear of the site has been noted for a second look when we return for the interviews.
Upcoming Work

Two tasks remain in the field and the record. We will complete the site interviews, including the current owner and a long-standing site manager, and we will make the follow-up visit to the rear equipment area to close out the photographic record.

The interviews are being scheduled now. We have the current owner lined up and are working through your team to reach a former site manager whose memory of the property runs back further than the written record. We expect to have both completed in the next few weeks.

James Henderson will then prepare the draft assessment to the ASTM E1527-13 standard. John Sanchez will review the findings before the report is finalized and signed, on the principle that no conclusion leaves this office until a second scientist has tested it against the record. Our aim for the next period is a complete draft ready for that review.
Items to Watch

Two things could affect the schedule, and we are managing both. The archived ownership records and the site-manager interview depend on materials and access from your side. The sooner we have them, the sooner we can close the interview stage.

The second is the up-gradient neighbor. If the file on that site raises a genuine question, we will report it as a recognized environmental condition and explain what, if anything, it would take to resolve it. We do not expect that outcome on what we have seen so far, but it would be premature to rule it out at the midpoint.

Nothing in the file to date changes our budget or our schedule. We raise these items because they are the ordinary places a Phase I slows down, not because either has slipped. If either does, you will hear it from us in the next report or sooner.

We will send the next report at the close of the coming period, or sooner if anything in the file warrants it. If you have questions in the meantime, please call and we will walk you through where things stand.
